claims.text: Theorem 1: for every k >= 1, (A^k)_ij is the number of walks of length k from n_i to n_j; proved by induction on k splitting walks by the last-but-one vertex. The textbook has no such theorem; the statement is in the Galway, Bai and Gotti sources.

support.quote: Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.

Thus the total number of walks of length k from vi to vj is the sum of the expressions (Ak−1)ir Arj over all vertices vr of G, which is exactly (Ak)ij.

The adjacency matrix is symmetric (i.e. equal to its transpose) if the graph is undirected. The adjacency matrix has zeros on its main diagonal (unless the graph has loops).

claims.text: Matrix powers of the board matrix: A^2 = [1 0 1; 0 2 0; 1 0 1], A^3 = [0 2 0; 2 0 2; 0 2 0], A^4 = [2 0 2; 0 4 0; 2 0 2]; each entry agrees with a brute-force walk enumeration for k = 1 to 4.

Walks versus paths in the board graph: (A^2)_11 = 1 counts the walk (n1,n2,n1), which is not a path; (A^3)_12 = 2 counts two walks and none is a path while exactly one path (length 1) joins n1 to n2; A^4 is nonzero although N - 1 = 2 bounds the length of paths.

support.quote: counts walks — not paths. This is because matrix multiplication accumulates all sequences of edges between two vertices, including those that revisit vertices and edges.
